hints: Look closely at Y and Z and notice exactly what changes and what stays the same.
Y has two different OH groups, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, but only the acid group is changed in Z.
Think about which reagents are selective for acids only, and which one is strong enough to attack the alcohol as well when in excess.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two functional groups in Y**

Y is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{H}$. It has an alcohol $-\text{OH}$ and a carboxylic acid $-\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.

Z is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CO}_2\text{Na}$. Only the acid has become its sodium salt, the alcohol is unchanged.

**Recall relative acidity**

Carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than alcohols. They react with metals, carbonates and hydroxides.

Alcohols are very weak acids. They react with reactive metals like $\text{Na}$, but not with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or $\text{NaOH}$.

**Test reagent 1, Na in excess**

$\text{Na}$ reacts with any $\text{O-H}$ bond to give $\text{H}_2$:
$$\text{RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + 1/2\text{H}_2$$
$$\text{ROH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{RONa} + 1/2\text{H}_2$$
In excess, both groups react to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(ONa)CO}_2\text{Na}$, not Z. So 1 is incorrect.

**Test reagents 2 and 3**

$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{NaOH}$ neutralise carboxylic acids but leave alcohols untouched:
$$2\text{RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Even in excess, the $\text{CH(OH)}$ group does not react. Both give exactly Z. So 2 and 3 are correct.

options.A: This means 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Reagents 2 and 3 do work, but 1 does not. Excess Na attacks both the acid and the alcohol, giving the disodium product, so this combination is wrong.
options.B: This means 1 and 2 only are correct. Reagent 2 is correct, but reagent 1 is wrong because Na is not selective. It will convert the alcohol to ONa as well as the acid to CO2Na.
options.C: This means 2 and 3 only are correct. Both Na2CO3 and NaOH are basic enough to deprotonate the carboxylic acid but not basic enough to deprotonate the alcohol, so even in excess they cleanly give CH3CH(OH)CO2Na.
options.D: This means 1 only is correct. Na alone cannot give Z selectively. It reacts vigorously with both acidic protons, so with excess you get reaction at both functional groups.
